Buffer held: 21 days. Supplier delay 42–63 days. Production stops 1–1 days for lack of the component (best known alternate starts day 35). Question: Walk through how the flood loss reaches Marlow Industries plc's balance sheet and covenants. Show your steps and give a verdict.

Sources:
[1] Scenario: Marlow Industries plc owns a food processing plant. Hazard: flood. All money is in millions of one currency.

[2] Financials before the event: revenue 2,353.9; EBITDA 536.1; net debt 255.5; interest expense 11.7; equity 1,307.2; total assets 3,464.4.

[3] Loss inputs: asset damage 1,167.6; insured recovery 462.0; lost revenue from interruption 77.5 at the company's average EBITDA margin; extra costs 38.5.

[4] Covenants: net debt/EBITDA at most 3.20x.

[5] Engine result, loss: uninsured asset loss 705.6; EBITDA hit 56.2; pre-tax loss 761.8, which is 142.1% of EBITDA; share of the loss that is uninsured 39.4%.

[6] Engine result, after the loss: EBITDA 479.9; net debt 1,017.3; net debt/EBITDA 2.12x (was 0.48x); EBITDA/interest 41.02x (was 45.82x); equity/total assets 23.7% (was 37.7%).

[7] Engine result, covenant tests: net debt/EBITDA 2.12x against a limit of at most 3.20x: pass, headroom 33.8%; before the loss it was a pass.

[8] Engine assumptions: the uninsured cash cost is funded by new debt; interest expense is unchanged; no covenant waiver, cure right, equity injection or insurer prepayment is assumed.

[9] Hurricane Harvey and the Arkema Crosby plant (case summary): the driver was record flooding from Hurricane Harvey; the exposed assets were the Arkema organic peroxide plant in Crosby and the Houston Ship Channel petrochemical complex; the event took place in North America in 2017.

[10] Hurricane Harvey and the Arkema Crosby plant (CBC): Flooding overwhelmed the Arkema Crosby plant's primary power supply and two emergency backups, so it lost refrigeration for its organic peroxides.

STEP 1 [FACT] Marlow Industries plc faces a flood loss with asset damage of 1,167.6, insured recovery of 462.0, 77.5 of lost revenue from interruption and extra costs of 38.5 [3].
STEP 2 [FACT] The engine puts the uninsured asset loss at 705.6 and the EBITDA hit at 56.2, so the pre-tax loss is 761.8, which is 142.1% of EBITDA [5].
STEP 3 [INFERENCE from 2] The loss is very large: it exceeds half a year of EBITDA; it is driven by uninsured damage, and insurance covers only part of the damage.
STEP 4 [FACT] After the loss EBITDA is 479.9 and net debt is 1,017.3; net debt/EBITDA moves from 0.48x to 2.12x [6].
STEP 5 [FACT] The net debt/EBITDA test is 2.12x against a limit of at most 3.20x: pass with headroom of 33.8%; before the loss it was a pass [7].
STEP 6 [INFERENCE from 5] Every covenant still passes with room to spare, so on these inputs the loss does not threaten the lending terms.
STEP 7 [PRECEDENT] In Hurricane Harvey and the Arkema Crosby plant: the driver was record flooding from Hurricane Harvey [9].
STEP 8 [INFERENCE from 7, 3] Analysis (not stated in the sources): past cases suggest checking physical damage to buildings and equipment, a shortage of an input such as power, water, transport or feedstock and legal liability and compensation claims as well as direct damage.
STEP 9 [CAVEAT] The engine assumes the uninsured cost is debt-funded and that no waiver, cure right or equity injection is available [8].
VERDICT: PASS
CHECK NEXT: whether the loss inputs are complete, for example other sites or interruption cover; also the policy limits and deductibles on the damaged assets.
NOT IN THE SOURCES: the insurer's payment timing, any covenant waiver, and the company's actual response.

Why validate a hazard model against historical events?

Validation shows whether a model reproduces what actually happened, such as observed storm tracks, recorded flood depths or tide-gauge levels, and how large the errors are. A model that cannot match the past gives little reason to trust its projections. Validation also reveals biases, such as consistent underestimation of extremes, which can then be corrected or reported. It does not prove future accuracy, but it limits the number of ways the model can be wrong.

Why is a 100-year flood a misleading name?

It describes a flood with a 1% chance of occurring in any year, not one that comes once a century. Two such floods can arrive in successive years, and over a 30-year mortgage the chance of at least one is about 26%. The estimate also changes as more data are collected and as the climate shifts, so a flood called a 100-year event today may be more frequent in future. The phrase 1% annual chance flood is clearer.

What is the social cost of carbon?

The social cost of carbon estimates the damage caused by emitting one additional tonne of carbon dioxide, expressed in money and discounted to today. It rests on climate, damage and discounting assumptions, so published figures range widely and are sensitive to the discount rate. What is the difference between storm surge and storm tide?

Storm surge is the rise of water above the normal tide caused by a storm's winds and low pressure. Storm tide is the total water level, the surge plus the astronomical tide. A modest surge arriving at high tide can flood far more than a larger surge at low tide, so the timing of a storm against the tidal cycle matters as much as its strength. Waves add a further rise on top of the still-water level at the shoreline.

What is average annual loss?

Average annual loss (AAL) is the long-run mean of the loss in a year, found by averaging over many simulated years, including the many years with no loss at all. It is the pure-risk part of a price: what an insurer expects to pay per year before expenses, profit and a margin for uncertainty. AAL is dominated by frequent moderate events, so it says little about the tail. Two portfolios with the same AAL can have very different 1-in-100 losses, which is why AAL is always reported next to exceedance-probability figures.

A regional air-quality model shows no skill at my site next to a cement works. What does that mean?

It means the model reproduces the regional background poorly or no better than a simple baseline, which is expected: a city-scale model averages over many kilometres and cannot see a stack or a quarry next door. It is not a statement that the air is clean. The right approach is to separate the measured regional record from the local sources, screen each source with a plume model using stated emission assumptions, and say plainly that only a monitor at the site settles the question.

What is double materiality?

Double materiality asks two questions about a sustainability topic: does it affect the company's financial position, and does the company affect people or the environment? A topic is reportable if either answer is yes. The European Sustainability Reporting Standards are built on it, whereas the ISSB standards focus on financial materiality, the first question only. For climate this means a company must disclose its own emissions impact as well as the financial risk climate poses to it.

Why does warming increase heavy rainfall?

Warmer air can hold about 7% more water vapour for each degree of warming, a relationship known as Clausius-Clapeyron. When storms form they can therefore deliver more rain per event, and the heaviest events often respond at or above that rate. This does not mean every place gets wetter: the total and the pattern of rainfall also depend on circulation. The engine uses ensemble ratios for extreme rain, which reflect both effects.

What are scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions?

Scope 1 is direct emissions from sources the company owns or controls, such as furnaces and vehicles. Scope 2 is indirect emissions from purchased electricity, heat or steam. Scope 3 is all other indirect emissions along the value chain, both upstream, such as purchased materials, and downstream, such as the use of sold products. Scope 3 is usually the largest and the hardest to measure, and the Greenhouse Gas Protocol sets the accounting rules for all three.

What does the p10 to p90 range mean?

When the same scenario is run through many climate models, each gives a slightly different result. The p10 to p90 range is the band that contains the middle 80% of those model results, with the median in the centre. It captures disagreement between models, not the full uncertainty: all models may share a bias, and natural variability adds noise on top. A narrow range means the models agree, not that the answer is certain.

What is double materiality?

Double materiality asks two questions about a sustainability topic: does it affect the company's financial position, and does the company affect people or the environment? A topic is reportable if either answer is yes. The European Sustainability Reporting Standards are built on it, whereas the ISSB standards focus on financial materiality, the first question only. For climate this means a company must disclose its own emissions impact as well as the financial risk climate poses to it.

What are the main types of flood?

River or fluvial flooding happens when a river exceeds its channel after prolonged or heavy rain upstream. Coastal flooding comes from storm surge and high tides pushing seawater onto land. Pluvial or surface-water flooding occurs when intense rain exceeds drainage capacity, even far from a river. Flash floods are fast, local floods from very intense rain or a dam failure. They need different data and defences, which is why a screening tool models them separately.

How does a deductible change the loss numbers?

A deductible removes the first slice of every loss, so it eliminates many small claims and cuts average annual loss sharply, but it hardly changes a very large event, where the deductible is a small part of the total. Deductibles therefore shape attritional cost and premium far more than they shape catastrophe capital.

Why is a 100-year flood a misleading name?

It describes a flood with a 1% chance of occurring in any year, not one that comes once a century. Two such floods can arrive in successive years, and over a 30-year mortgage the chance of at least one is about 26%. The estimate also changes as more data are collected and as the climate shifts, so a flood called a 100-year event today may be more frequent in future. The phrase 1% annual chance flood is clearer.

What is UTCI and why does the engine build it itself?

The Universal Thermal Climate Index is the temperature of a reference calm, mild outdoor condition that would put the same thermal strain on a person as the real combination of air temperature, humidity, wind and radiation. It covers cold stress as well as heat stress. Published archives cover a limited period and cannot be queried for any coordinate, so the engine builds the index from hourly reanalysis weather for the place, from 1981 to within days of today, and counts the hours in each stress category. It is not a measured quantity, and the engine says how far it agreed with weather stations.

What does the delayed-transition scenario assume?

It assumes climate policy is weak until about 2030 and then tightens abruptly to meet the same long-run temperature goal. The late start means a steeper and more disruptive rise in carbon prices and sharper effects on high-emission sectors, even though the end temperature may be similar to an orderly path. It is used to test how exposed a company is to a sudden policy shift, which tends to hit the highest-carbon assets hardest.

What is an SSP?

A Shared Socioeconomic Pathway describes how population, economy, energy use and policy might evolve, and each is paired with a radiative-forcing level to make a climate scenario such as SSP2-4.5. The number after the hyphen is the approximate extra forcing in watts per square metre by 2100. The IPCC's sixth assessment gives best estimates of warming for 2081 to 2100 relative to 1850 to 1900 of about 1.8 degrees for SSP1-2.6, 2.7 for SSP2-4.5, 3.6 for SSP3-7.0 and 4.4 for SSP5-8.5.

What is average annual loss?

Average annual loss (AAL) is the long-run mean of the loss in a year, found by averaging over many simulated years, including the many years with no loss at all. It is the pure-risk part of a price: what an insurer expects to pay per year before expenses, profit and a margin for uncertainty. AAL is dominated by frequent moderate events, so it says little about the tail. Two portfolios with the same AAL can have very different 1-in-100 losses, which is why AAL is always reported next to exceedance-probability figures.

What does attribution mean when a source says an event was made more likely by climate change?

Attribution studies compare the chance of an event in today's climate with its chance in a world without human influence, using models and observations. A statement that climate change made it, for example, twice as likely is a statement about probability, not about cause in a single case. Results depend on the event definition and on how well models represent that weather type, so confidence is higher for heat than for convective rain.

What is accumulation and why does it matter?

Accumulation is the build-up of exposure that can be hit by a single event, such as all insured sites inside one cyclone's wind field or one river basin. It matters because losses from nearby sites move together, so the tail of a portfolio is driven by concentration, not by the number of policies. Insurers monitor accumulation by zone, country and peril and set limits on each, because an event in the densest zone can erase many years of premium.

What is accumulation and why does it matter?

Accumulation is the build-up of exposure that can be hit by a single event, such as all insured sites inside one cyclone's wind field or one river basin. It matters because losses from nearby sites move together, so the tail of a portfolio is driven by concentration, not by the number of policies. Insurers monitor accumulation by zone, country and peril and set limits on each, because an event in the densest zone can erase many years of premium.

Why are return periods flagged as not reliable?

A simulation can only estimate a return period well if it has enough years to see events of that size several times. A common rule is to require at least ten simulated years per year of return period, so 5,000 years supports return periods up to about 500 years, and 1-in-1,000 would need 10,000 years. Beyond that the estimate rests on one or two simulated years and can move a lot with the random seed, so the engine marks it rather than presenting false precision.

What is secondary uncertainty?

Secondary uncertainty is the spread of possible damage given that an event of a certain intensity has occurred. Two buildings facing the same wind speed or flood depth do not suffer the same percentage damage. Models that use only a mean damage curve understate the tail because some buildings do far worse than average. Including it generally raises extreme losses while leaving the average nearly unchanged.

What are scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions?

Scope 1 is direct emissions from sources the company owns or controls, such as furnaces and vehicles. Scope 2 is indirect emissions from purchased electricity, heat or steam. Scope 3 is all other indirect emissions along the value chain, both upstream, such as purchased materials, and downstream, such as the use of sold products. Scope 3 is usually the largest and the hardest to measure, and the Greenhouse Gas Protocol sets the accounting rules for all three.

What is UTCI and why does the engine build it itself?

The Universal Thermal Climate Index is the temperature of a reference calm, mild outdoor condition that would put the same thermal strain on a person as the real combination of air temperature, humidity, wind and radiation. It covers cold stress as well as heat stress. Published archives cover a limited period and cannot be queried for any coordinate, so the engine builds the index from hourly reanalysis weather for the place, from 1981 to within days of today, and counts the hours in each stress category. It is not a measured quantity, and the engine says how far it agreed with weather stations.

What is the model-uncertainty load?

It is a percentage added to expected loss to reflect that the model itself may be wrong: hazard maps are imperfect, damage functions are not calibrated to claims, and the number of simulated years is finite. A larger load is appropriate when data are thin or the peril is poorly constrained. It is a judgement, not a measurement, which is why the engine shows it as an explicit parameter instead of burying it inside the loss figures.

What is a reinstatement?

A reinstatement restores the limit of an excess-of-loss layer after it has been used, so the layer can respond again in the same period. Each reinstatement usually costs an additional premium, often a share of the original premium in proportion to the limit used. A layer with one reinstatement can pay up to twice its limit across the year. In a simulation, reinstatements matter in years with several large events, so they affect the aggregate result more than the occurrence result.

Why does sea-level rise matter more than its size suggests?

A modest rise lifts the whole baseline on which tides and surges ride, so a surge that used to be rare reaches the same height far more often. Return periods of coastal floods shrink faster than the sea-level numbers imply. Local land subsidence can add as much as the global rise, and the global figure hides large regional differences, which is why local sea-level and land-motion data are preferable when they exist.

What is the difference between storm surge and storm tide?

Storm surge is the rise of water above the normal tide caused by a storm's winds and low pressure. Storm tide is the total water level, the surge plus the astronomical tide. A modest surge arriving at high tide can flood far more than a larger surge at low tide, so the timing of a storm against the tidal cycle matters as much as its strength. Waves add a further rise on top of the still-water level at the shoreline.

Why is flood loss sometimes near zero at a site that is known to flood?

What is the difference between occurrence and aggregate exceedance probability?

Occurrence exceedance probability (OEP) looks at the single largest loss in each year and asks how often that largest event exceeds a given size. Aggregate exceedance probability (AEP) looks at the total of all losses in the year. AEP is always at least as large as OEP at the same probability. For a book dominated by one huge event per year they are nearly identical; when several moderate events can stack, AEP pulls ahead. Occurrence curves suit per-event reinsurance, aggregate curves suit annual capital and stop-loss covers.

How does the EU Emissions Trading System work?

The EU ETS is a cap-and-trade system: it sets a limit on emissions from covered installations, issues or auctions allowances up to that limit, and requires each installation to surrender one allowance for each tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent emitted. The cap falls over time, which raises scarcity and the price. Companies that cut emissions cheaply can sell spare allowances; those that cannot must buy them, which is how the system reveals the cost of abatement.

What are scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions?

Scope 1 is direct emissions from sources the company owns or controls, such as furnaces and vehicles. Scope 2 is indirect emissions from purchased electricity, heat or steam. Scope 3 is all other indirect emissions along the value chain, both upstream, such as purchased materials, and downstream, such as the use of sold products. Scope 3 is usually the largest and the hardest to measure, and the Greenhouse Gas Protocol sets the accounting rules for all three.

What is the CSRD?

The Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive, Directive (EU) 2022/2464, requires in-scope companies to publish sustainability information in their management report using the European Sustainability Reporting Standards, with limited assurance. Scope, thresholds and timing have been revised by later EU simplification measures, so applicability to a given company should be checked against the current text. For climate the key standard is ESRS E1, which covers transition plans, targets, emissions and climate risk.

What is the model-uncertainty load?

It is a percentage added to expected loss to reflect that the model itself may be wrong: hazard maps are imperfect, damage functions are not calibrated to claims, and the number of simulated years is finite. A larger load is appropriate when data are thin or the peril is poorly constrained. It is a judgement, not a measurement, which is why the engine shows it as an explicit parameter instead of burying it inside the loss figures.

Why does spatial correlation change the tail but not the average?

The average loss is a sum of expectations, and expectations add up whether sites are correlated or not. The tail is different: when sites share the same storm or flood season they tend to be hit together, so bad years become worse and good years better, widening the distribution. Raising the correlation length therefore leaves AAL almost unchanged but raises the 1-in-100 loss and tail value at risk. Correlation lengths are assumptions unless fitted to event footprints, so they should be tested at low, base and high settings.

What is the difference between physical risk and transition risk?

Physical risk is damage from climate hazards: acute events such as floods and storms, and chronic changes such as heat and sea-level rise. Transition risk is financial exposure to the shift to a low-carbon economy through carbon prices, regulation, technology and changing demand. They interact: a low-emission pathway reduces long-run physical damage but raises transition risk early, while a high-emission pathway does the opposite. Credible analysis treats the two as a pair under the same scenario.

Hurricane Warning: An announcement that sustained winds of 64 knots (74 mph or 119 km/hr) or higher are expected somewhere within the specified area in association with a tropical , subtropical , or post-tropical cyclone. Because hurricane preparedness activities become difficult once winds reach tropical storm force, the warning is issued 36 hours in advance of the anticipated onset of tropical-storm-force winds. Why would an insurer run 20,000 simulated years instead of 5,000?

More years shrink the sampling error of the average and make the tail estimates steadier. The average loss converges fairly quickly because it uses every year; tail figures converge slowly because only a few years sit beyond the threshold. Going from 5,000 to 20,000 years roughly halves the standard error of the average and extends reliable return periods. It costs run time, so the choice is a trade-off between precision and speed for the decision at hand.

Does the Saffir-Simpson category tell me how much flooding to expect?

No. The Saffir-Simpson scale rates a hurricane by its maximum sustained wind speed only. Storm surge depends also on the storm's size, forward speed, angle of approach and the shape of the coastline and sea floor, and rainfall flooding depends on how fast the storm moves and how much water it carries. A lower-category storm can produce more surge or inland flooding than a higher one, so wind category should not be used as a flood forecast.

What does the capital proxy in the premium represent?

It estimates how much capital the site ties up: the site's average loss in the worst 1% of portfolio years minus its average loss. Capital is held for bad years, so a site that tends to lose most when the whole portfolio is having a bad year uses more capital than a site with the same average loss that fails independently. The cost of capital is applied to this amount, which is why two sites with similar AAL can carry different premiums.

Question: What should I know about safety information?

Sources:
[1] NOAA NHC: Glossary of terms: A term used in NWS advisory products to describe a disturbance that is not yet a tropical cyclone , but which poses the threat of bringing tropical storm or hurricane conditions to land areas within 72 hours. Preliminary Report: Now known as the "Tropical Cyclone Report". A report summarizing the life history and effects of an Atlantic or eastern Pacific tropical cyclone . It contains a summary of the cyclone life cycle and pertinent meteorological data, including the post-analysis best track (six-hourly positions and intensities) and other meteorological statistics. It also contains a description of damage and casualties the system produced, as well as information on forecasts and warnings associated with the cyclone. NHC writes a report on every tropical cyclone in its area of responsibility.

[2] NWS: Heat safety: NWS Safety information on Children, Pets and Vehicles: It is NEVER safe to leave a child, disabled person or pet locked in a car, even in the winter. If you have a toddler in your household, lock your cars, even in your own driveway. Kids may play in cars or wander outside and get into a car and can die in 10 minutes! A reported 31 children died in hot cars in 2025. To see the latest information, go to this link . Deaths routinely are reported as early as April and tragedies continue into December in southern states.

[3] NOAA NHC: Glossary of terms: Tropical Storm Warning: An announcement that sustained winds of 34 to 63 knots (39 to 73 mph or 63 to 118 km/hr) are expected somewhere within the specified area within 36 hours in association with a tropical , subtropical , or post-tropical cyclone. Tropical Storm Watch: An announcement that sustained winds of 34 to 63 knots (39 to 73 mph or 63 to 118 km/hr) are possible within the specified area within 48 hours in association with a tropical , subtropical , or post-tropical cyclone. Tropical Wave: A trough or cyclonic curvature maximum in the trade-wind easterlies. The wave may reach maximum amplitude in the lower middle troposphere.

[4] NOAA NHC: Glossary of terms: Storm Surge Warning: The danger of life-threatening inundation from rising water moving inland from the shoreline somewhere within the specified area, generally within 36 hours, in association with an ongoing or potential tropical cyclones , a subtropical cyclone or a post-tropical cyclone . The warning may be issued earlier when other conditions, such as the onset of tropical-storm -force winds are expected to limit the time available to take protective actions for surge (e.g., evacuations). The warning may also be issued for locations not expected to receive life-threatening inundation but which could potentially be isolated by inundation in adjacent areas.

[5] NOAA NHC: Glossary of terms: The flooding of normally dry land, primarily caused by severe weather events along the coasts, estuaries, and adjoining rivers. These storms, which include hurricanes and nor'easters, bring strong winds and heavy rains. The winds drive large waves and storm surge on shore, and heavy rains raise rivers. (A tsunami — a giant wave caused by earthquakes or volcanic eruptions under the sea or landslides into the sea — is another kind of coastal inundation, but should not be confused with storm surge.) Landfall: The intersection of the surface center of a tropical cyclone with a coastline. Because the strongest winds in a tropical cyclone are not located precisely at the center, it is possible for a cyclone's strongest winds to be experienced over land even if landfall does not occur. Similarly, it is possible for a tropical cyclone to make landfall and have its strongest winds remain over the water. Compare direct hit , indirect hit , and strike .

What is the difference between physical risk and transition risk?

Physical risk is damage from climate hazards: acute events such as floods and storms, and chronic changes such as heat and sea-level rise. Transition risk is financial exposure to the shift to a low-carbon economy through carbon prices, regulation, technology and changing demand. They interact: a low-emission pathway reduces long-run physical damage but raises transition risk early, while a high-emission pathway does the opposite. Credible analysis treats the two as a pair under the same scenario.

Does the Saffir-Simpson category tell me how much flooding to expect?

No. The Saffir-Simpson scale rates a hurricane by its maximum sustained wind speed only. Storm surge depends also on the storm's size, forward speed, angle of approach and the shape of the coastline and sea floor, and rainfall flooding depends on how fast the storm moves and how much water it carries. A lower-category storm can produce more surge or inland flooding than a higher one, so wind category should not be used as a flood forecast.

What are the main types of flood?

River or fluvial flooding happens when a river exceeds its channel after prolonged or heavy rain upstream. Coastal flooding comes from storm surge and high tides pushing seawater onto land. Pluvial or surface-water flooding occurs when intense rain exceeds drainage capacity, even far from a river. Flash floods are fast, local floods from very intense rain or a dam failure. They need different data and defences, which is why a screening tool models them separately.

What are the main types of flood?

River or fluvial flooding happens when a river exceeds its channel after prolonged or heavy rain upstream. Coastal flooding comes from storm surge and high tides pushing seawater onto land. Pluvial or surface-water flooding occurs when intense rain exceeds drainage capacity, even far from a river. Flash floods are fast, local floods from very intense rain or a dam failure. They need different data and defences, which is why a screening tool models them separately.

Why does warming increase heavy rainfall?

Warmer air can hold about 7% more water vapour for each degree of warming, a relationship known as Clausius-Clapeyron. When storms form they can therefore deliver more rain per event, and the heaviest events often respond at or above that rate. This does not mean every place gets wetter: the total and the pattern of rainfall also depend on circulation. The engine uses ensemble ratios for extreme rain, which reflect both effects.

Why are return periods flagged as not reliable?

A simulation can only estimate a return period well if it has enough years to see events of that size several times. A common rule is to require at least ten simulated years per year of return period, so 5,000 years supports return periods up to about 500 years, and 1-in-1,000 would need 10,000 years. Beyond that the estimate rests on one or two simulated years and can move a lot with the random seed, so the engine marks it rather than presenting false precision.

How is ISSB IFRS S2 different from ESRS E1?

IFRS S2 follows the four pillars of the earlier TCFD recommendations: governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets. It is investor-focused and uses financial materiality. ESRS E1 is broader because it rests on double materiality and asks for more granular data points. The two share much content on scenario analysis and emissions, and many companies map one to the other to avoid duplicate work, but a disclosure prepared for one does not automatically satisfy the other.

What is the social cost of carbon?

The social cost of carbon estimates the damage caused by emitting one additional tonne of carbon dioxide, expressed in money and discounted to today. It rests on climate, damage and discounting assumptions, so published figures range widely and are sensitive to the discount rate. It is a policy tool for weighing regulations, not a market price, and should not be mixed with the price of allowances in a trading system.

Why would an insurer run 20,000 simulated years instead of 5,000?

More years shrink the sampling error of the average and make the tail estimates steadier. The average loss converges fairly quickly because it uses every year; tail figures converge slowly because only a few years sit beyond the threshold. Going from 5,000 to 20,000 years roughly halves the standard error of the average and extends reliable return periods. It costs run time, so the choice is a trade-off between precision and speed for the decision at hand.

What is secondary uncertainty?

Secondary uncertainty is the spread of possible damage given that an event of a certain intensity has occurred. Two buildings facing the same wind speed or flood depth do not suffer the same percentage damage. Models that use only a mean damage curve understate the tail because some buildings do far worse than average. Including it generally raises extreme losses while leaving the average nearly unchanged.

Why does spatial correlation change the tail but not the average?

The average loss is a sum of expectations, and expectations add up whether sites are correlated or not. The tail is different: when sites share the same storm or flood season they tend to be hit together, so bad years become worse and good years better, widening the distribution. Raising the correlation length therefore leaves AAL almost unchanged but raises the 1-in-100 loss and tail value at risk. Correlation lengths are assumptions unless fitted to event footprints, so they should be tested at low, base and high settings.

What is the difference between physical risk and transition risk?

Physical risk is damage from climate hazards: acute events such as floods and storms, and chronic changes such as heat and sea-level rise. Transition risk is financial exposure to the shift to a low-carbon economy through carbon prices, regulation, technology and changing demand. They interact: a low-emission pathway reduces long-run physical damage but raises transition risk early, while a high-emission pathway does the opposite. Credible analysis treats the two as a pair under the same scenario.

How do quota share and excess-of-loss reinsurance differ?

Quota share cedes a fixed percentage of every loss, so it scales the whole distribution down and reduces average loss and tail alike in proportion. Excess-of-loss reinsurance pays only the part of a loss above an attachment point up to a limit, so it leaves small losses with the insurer and protects against big ones. Reinstatements allow a layer's limit to be restored after a payment, usually for an extra premium. Quota share is simple capital relief; excess of loss is targeted tail protection.

This annual report , provides a comprehensive accounting of total greenhouse gas emissions for all man-made sources in the United States, including carbon dioxide removal from the atmosphere by “sinks,” (e.g., through the uptake of carbon and storage in forests, vegetation, and soils) from management of lands in their current use or as lands are converted to other uses. The gases covered by the Inventory include carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, hydrofluorocarbons, perfluorocarbons, sulfur hexafluoride, and nitrogen trifluoride. The national greenhouse gas inventory is submitted to the United Nations in accordance with the Framework Convention on Climate Change . In preparing the annual emissions and sinks inventory report, EPA collaborates with hundreds of experts representing more than a dozen U.S. government agencies, academic institutions, industry associations, consultants and environmental organizations. What is a marginal abatement cost curve?

A marginal abatement cost curve ranks emission-reduction measures from cheapest to most expensive per tonne of carbon dioxide avoided, with the width of each bar showing how many tonnes it removes. Measures with negative cost save money over their life. Comparing the curve with a carbon price shows which measures pay for themselves at that price and how much abatement is economic. The costs depend heavily on assumptions about energy prices, discount rates and technology.

How does a deductible change the loss numbers?

A deductible removes the first slice of every loss, so it eliminates many small claims and cuts average annual loss sharply, but it hardly changes a very large event, where the deductible is a small part of the total. Deductibles therefore shape attritional cost and premium far more than they shape catastrophe capital.

What is average annual loss?

Average annual loss (AAL) is the long-run mean of the loss in a year, found by averaging over many simulated years, including the many years with no loss at all. It is the pure-risk part of a price: what an insurer expects to pay per year before expenses, profit and a margin for uncertainty. AAL is dominated by frequent moderate events, so it says little about the tail. Two portfolios with the same AAL can have very different 1-in-100 losses, which is why AAL is always reported next to exceedance-probability figures.

What does the capital proxy in the premium represent?

It estimates how much capital the site ties up: the site's average loss in the worst 1% of portfolio years minus its average loss. Capital is held for bad years, so a site that tends to lose most when the whole portfolio is having a bad year uses more capital than a site with the same average loss that fails independently. The cost of capital is applied to this amount, which is why two sites with similar AAL can carry different premiums.

Why do the scenarios look so similar before 2050?

Climate responds slowly to emissions because of the heat stored in the oceans and the long life of carbon dioxide in the air. Warming through the 2030s and 2040s is largely locked in by past emissions, so the pathways diverge mainly in the second half of the century. Why would an insurer run 20,000 simulated years instead of 5,000?

More years shrink the sampling error of the average and make the tail estimates steadier. The average loss converges fairly quickly because it uses every year; tail figures converge slowly because only a few years sit beyond the threshold. Going from 5,000 to 20,000 years roughly halves the standard error of the average and extends reliable return periods. It costs run time, so the choice is a trade-off between precision and speed for the decision at hand.

What is a stranded asset?

A stranded asset is an asset that loses value before the end of its expected life because of changes tied to climate, such as a carbon price, a ban, falling demand or physical damage that makes it uneconomic. Coal plants and high-carbon industrial plants are classic transition examples; a coastal facility that can no longer be insured or defended is a physical one. The size of the loss depends on how fast the change comes and on the remaining book life.

What does the p10 to p90 range mean?

When the same scenario is run through many climate models, each gives a slightly different result. The p10 to p90 range is the band that contains the middle 80% of those model results, with the median in the centre. It captures disagreement between models, not the full uncertainty: all models may share a bias, and natural variability adds noise on top. A narrow range means the models agree, not that the answer is certain.

How does the EU Emissions Trading System work?

The EU ETS is a cap-and-trade system: it sets a limit on emissions from covered installations, issues or auctions allowances up to that limit, and requires each installation to surrender one allowance for each tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent emitted. The cap falls over time, which raises scarcity and the price. Companies that cut emissions cheaply can sell spare allowances; those that cannot must buy them, which is how the system reveals the cost of abatement.

Question: What should I know about water vapor?

Sources:
[1] EPA: Overview of greenhouse gases: Concentration, or abundance, is the amount of a particular gas in the air. Larger emissions of greenhouse gases lead to higher concentrations in the atmosphere. Greenhouse gas concentrations are measured in parts per million, parts per billion, and even parts per trillion. One part per million is equivalent to one drop of water diluted into about 13 gallons of liquid (roughly the fuel tank of a compact car). To learn more about the increasing concentrations of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, visit the Climate Change Indicators: Atmospheric Concentrations of Greenhouse Gases page. How long do greenhouse gases stay in the atmosphere? Each of these gases can remain in the atmosphere for different amounts of time, ranging from a few years to thousands of years. All these gases remain in the atmosphere long enough to become well mixed, meaning that the amount that is measured in the atmosphere is roughly the same all over the world, regardless of the source of the emissions. How strongly do greenhouse gases impact the atmosphere? Some gases are more effective than others at making the planet warmer and "thickening the Earth's atmospheric blanket." For each greenhouse gas, a Global Warming Potential (GWP) was developed to allow comparisons of the global warming impacts of different gases. Specifically, it is a measure of how much energy the emissions of 1 ton of a gas will absorb over a given period of time, typically a 100-year time horizon, relative to the emissions of 1 ton of carbon dioxide (CO 2 ). Gases with a higher GWP absorb more energy, per ton emitted, than gases with a lower GWP, and thus contribute more to warming Earth. Note: All emission estimates are sourced from the Inventory of U.S. Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Sinks: 1990–2022 . The Inventory uses 100-year GWPs from IPCC’s Fifth Assessment Report (AR5). Explanation of Units A million metric tons of CO2: What does that mean? A million metric tons equals about 2.2 billion pounds, or 1 trillion grams. For comparison, a small car is likely to weigh a little more than 1 metric ton. Thus, a million metric tons is roughly the same mass as 1 million small cars! The U.S. GHG Inventory uses metric units for consistency and comparability with other countries. For reference, a metric ton is slightly more (approximately 10%) than a U.S. "short" ton. GHG emissions are often measured in carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) equivalent. To convert emissions of a gas into CO 2 equivalent, its emissions are multiplied by the gas's Global Warming Potential (GWP) . The GWP takes into account the fact that many gases are more effective at warming Earth than CO 2 , per unit mass. The GWP values appearing in the Overview of Greenhouse Gases and Sources of Greenhouse Gas web pages reflect the values used in the U.S. GHG Inventory, which are drawn from the IPCC’s Fifth Assessment Report (AR5). For further discussion of GWPs and an estimate of GHG emissions using updated GWPs, see Annex 6 of the U.S. GHG Inventory and the IPCC's discussion on GWPs (pdf) .

[2] EPA: Overview of greenhouse gases: Greenhouse Gas Emissions Overview, by Type of Gas: 2022 Total U.S. Emissions in 2022 = 6,343 Million Metric Tons of CO₂ equivalent (excludes land sector). Percentages may not add up to 100% due to independent rounding. Land Use, Land-Use Change, and Forestry in the United States is a net sink and offsets 13% of these greenhouse gas emissions. Question: What should I know about subtropical cyclone?

Sources:
[1] NOAA NHC: Glossary of terms: Subtropical Depression: A subtropical cyclone in which the maximum sustained surface wind speed (using the U.S. 1-minute average) is 33 kt (38 mph or 62 km/hr) or less. Subtropical Storm: A subtropical cyclone in which the maximum sustained surface wind speed (using the U.S. 1-minute average) is 34 kt (39 mph or 63 km/hr) or more. Synoptic Track: Weather reconnaissance mission flown to provide vital meteorological information in data sparse ocean areas as a supplement to existing surface, radar, and satellite data. Synoptic flights better define the upper atmosphere and aid in the prediction of tropical cyclone development and movement.

[2] NOAA NHC: Storm surge overview: Surge animation of a small storm vs. a large storm pushing water (Click on image to play video) The angle at which a storm approaches a coastline can affect the amount of storm surge pushed over land. A storm that moves onshore perpendicular to the coast is more likely to produce a higher storm surge than one that moves parallel to the coast or inland at an oblique angle. The image on the left shows a storm approaching at an angle; however, the image on the right shows a storm approaching nearly perpendicular to the coastline. Areas highlighted in red and orange increase around Staten Island and along the banks of the Hudson River between New Jersey and New York.

[3] NOAA NHC: Storm surge overview: NATIONAL HURRICANE CENTER and CENTRAL PACIFIC HURRICANE CENTER Storm Surge Unit | Surge Overview | National Surge Hazard Maps | International Surge Viewer | Operational Products | Resources Storm Surge can be Dangerous or Life-Threatening Storm surge from tropical cyclones poses a significant threat to life and property along the coast and is currently the leading cause of fatalities from hurricanes. All locations along the U.S. East and Gulf coasts are vulnerable to storm surges. Storm surge can even travel up rivers and canals, reaching well inland from the coastline. The impacts from Hurricane Ian (2022) are a reminder of the widespread devastation storm surge can cause, attributing to 41 lives lost. Awareness of the destructive potential of storm surge is crucial for improving safety and resilience in coastal communities.

[4] NOAA NHC: Storm surge overview: Shape of the Coastline and Local Features Storm surge will be higher when a storm makes landfall on a concave coastline (curved inward, such as Apalachee Bay in Florida) than a convex coastline (curved outward, such as the Outer Banks of North Carolina). Storm surge is also highly dependent on local features and barriers that affect the flow of water. A good example is the coast of North Carolina, which has complex features such as barrier islands, inlets, sounds, bays, and rivers. In reality, storm surge only makes up a part of what causes water levels to rise along the coast during a hurricane. Tides, wave setup, and freshwater flow all contribute to the total water level rise.

[5] NOAA NHC: Storm surge overview: Storm Surge can be Dangerous or Life-Threatening Adding to the destructive power of surge, battering waves may increase damage to buildings directly along the coast. Water weighs approximately 1,700 pounds per cubic yard; extended pounding by frequent waves can demolish any structure not specifically designed to withstand such forces. The two elements work together to increase the impact on land because the surge allows waves to extend inland. Additionally, currents created by tides combine with the waves to severely erode beaches and coastal highways. Buildings that survive hurricane winds can be damaged if erosion undermines and weakens their foundations. In confined harbors, the combination of storm tides, waves, and currents can also severely damage marinas and boats. Saltwater intrusion in estuaries and bayous endangers public health, kills vegetation, and can send animals, such as snakes and alligators, fleeing from flooded areas.

Why does warming increase heavy rainfall?

Warmer air can hold about 7% more water vapour for each degree of warming, a relationship known as Clausius-Clapeyron. When storms form they can therefore deliver more rain per event, and the heaviest events often respond at or above that rate. This does not mean every place gets wetter: the total and the pattern of rainfall also depend on circulation. The engine uses ensemble ratios for extreme rain, which reflect both effects.

Does the Saffir-Simpson category tell me how much flooding to expect?

No. The Saffir-Simpson scale rates a hurricane by its maximum sustained wind speed only. Storm surge depends also on the storm's size, forward speed, angle of approach and the shape of the coastline and sea floor, and rainfall flooding depends on how fast the storm moves and how much water it carries. A lower-category storm can produce more surge or inland flooding than a higher one, so wind category should not be used as a flood forecast.

What is the social cost of carbon?

The social cost of carbon estimates the damage caused by emitting one additional tonne of carbon dioxide, expressed in money and discounted to today. It rests on climate, damage and discounting assumptions, so published figures range widely and are sensitive to the discount rate. It is a policy tool for weighing regulations, not a market price, and should not be mixed with the price of allowances in a trading system.

Why does sea-level rise matter more than its size suggests?

A modest rise lifts the whole baseline on which tides and surges ride, so a surge that used to be rare reaches the same height far more often. Return periods of coastal floods shrink faster than the sea-level numbers imply. Local land subsidence can add as much as the global rise, and the global figure hides large regional differences, which is why local sea-level and land-motion data are preferable when they exist.

What does the p10 to p90 range mean?

When the same scenario is run through many climate models, each gives a slightly different result. The p10 to p90 range is the band that contains the middle 80% of those model results, with the median in the centre. It captures disagreement between models, not the full uncertainty: all models may share a bias, and natural variability adds noise on top. A narrow range means the models agree, not that the answer is certain.

What is CBAM?

The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, Regulation (EU) 2023/956, puts a carbon price on certain imports so that they bear a cost comparable to EU producers under the Emissions Trading System. It covers cement, iron and steel, aluminium, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen. A reporting-only transitional period ran from October 2023 through 2025, and the financial obligation to surrender certificates starts with the definitive period from 2026. Thresholds and rules have been changing, so current conditions should be checked.

What is the difference between storm surge and storm tide?

Storm surge is the rise of water above the normal tide caused by a storm's winds and low pressure. Storm tide is the total water level, the surge plus the astronomical tide. A modest surge arriving at high tide can flood far more than a larger surge at low tide, so the timing of a storm against the tidal cycle matters as much as its strength. Waves add a further rise on top of the still-water level at the shoreline.

What is a marginal abatement cost curve?

A marginal abatement cost curve ranks emission-reduction measures from cheapest to most expensive per tonne of carbon dioxide avoided, with the width of each bar showing how many tonnes it removes. Measures with negative cost save money over their life. Comparing the curve with a carbon price shows which measures pay for themselves at that price and how much abatement is economic. The costs depend heavily on assumptions about energy prices, discount rates and technology.

What is secondary uncertainty?

Secondary uncertainty is the spread of possible damage given that an event of a certain intensity has occurred. Two buildings facing the same wind speed or flood depth do not suffer the same percentage damage. Models that use only a mean damage curve understate the tail because some buildings do far worse than average. Including it generally raises extreme losses while leaving the average nearly unchanged.

What does a 1-in-100 loss mean?

A 1-in-100 loss is the loss level with a 1% chance of being exceeded in any one year. It does not mean the loss happens once every hundred years, and it does not mean it cannot happen twice in a decade. Over a 30-year horizon the chance of at least one such year is roughly one in four. Insurers often call the occurrence version the probable maximum loss, but the term has no single legal definition, so always state whether the figure is occurrence or aggregate.

How is ISSB IFRS S2 different from ESRS E1?

IFRS S2 follows the four pillars of the earlier TCFD recommendations: governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets. It is investor-focused and uses financial materiality. ESRS E1 is broader because it rests on double materiality and asks for more granular data points. The two share much content on scenario analysis and emissions, and many companies map one to the other to avoid duplicate work, but a disclosure prepared for one does not automatically satisfy the other.

Why is flood loss sometimes near zero at a site that is known to flood?

Because a mapped flood hazard layer only shows depths at the resolution and return periods it was built for, and defences or elevation may keep a small footprint dry in the map. Coarse river maps and coastal layers can miss local drainage and surface-water flooding. A near-zero modelled flood loss is therefore a statement about the map, not a guarantee of safety. A site-specific hydraulic study or a local flood-depth survey is the right way to test it.

Why are stack emissions from a compliant cement works only a small part of the particle problem near it?

A tall stack with a filter at its legal limit releases modest amounts, and the plume mixes before it reaches the ground, so its annual contribution at a few kilometres is often a fraction of one microgram per cubic metre to a few. Much of the local burden usually comes from fugitive sources: the quarry, crushers, stockpiles, conveyors and haul roads, which are low-level and uncontrolled. A stack-only screen is therefore a lower bound for coarse particles, and the engine says so.

What does attribution mean when a source says an event was made more likely by climate change?

Attribution studies compare the chance of an event in today's climate with its chance in a world without human influence, using models and observations. A statement that climate change made it, for example, twice as likely is a statement about probability, not about cause in a single case. Results depend on the event definition and on how well models represent that weather type, so confidence is higher for heat than for convective rain.

Why validate a hazard model against historical events?

Validation shows whether a model reproduces what actually happened, such as observed storm tracks, recorded flood depths or tide-gauge levels, and how large the errors are. A model that cannot match the past gives little reason to trust its projections. Validation also reveals biases, such as consistent underestimation of extremes, which can then be corrected or reported. It does not prove future accuracy, but it limits the number of ways the model can be wrong.

What is a reinstatement?

A reinstatement restores the limit of an excess-of-loss layer after it has been used, so the layer can respond again in the same period. Each reinstatement usually costs an additional premium, often a share of the original premium in proportion to the limit used. What is double materiality?

Double materiality asks two questions about a sustainability topic: does it affect the company's financial position, and does the company affect people or the environment? A topic is reportable if either answer is yes. The European Sustainability Reporting Standards are built on it, whereas the ISSB standards focus on financial materiality, the first question only. For climate this means a company must disclose its own emissions impact as well as the financial risk climate poses to it.

The data have been smoothed using a 5-day running average centered on each calendar day. For the Atlantic basin (the Atlantic Ocean, the Caribbean Sea, and the Gulf of America), the chart is based on data from the 77-year period from 1944 to 2020 (starting at the beginning of the aircraft reconnaissance era) but normalized to 100 years. The official hurricane season for the Atlantic basin is from June 1 to November 30, but tropical cyclone activity sometimes occurs before and after these dates, respectively. The peak of the Atlantic hurricane season is September 10, with most activity occurring between mid-August and mid-October. For the eastern Pacific basin, the analyses are based on data from the 50-year period from 1971 to 2020 (starting when there was reliable satellite imagery) but also normalized to 100 years. The official hurricane season for the eastern Pacific basin is from May 15 to November 30, but tropical cyclones occasionally occur before and after these dates, respectively. A peak in activity is noted in late August, but this peak is less pronounced than the peak in Atlantic activity. Relatively high levels of activity in the eastern Pacific tend to be spread out over a longer portion of the season than in the Atlantic, with most tropical cyclones occurring between late June and early October.

How does the EU Emissions Trading System work?

The EU ETS is a cap-and-trade system: it sets a limit on emissions from covered installations, issues or auctions allowances up to that limit, and requires each installation to surrender one allowance for each tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent emitted. The cap falls over time, which raises scarcity and the price. Companies that cut emissions cheaply can sell spare allowances; those that cannot must buy them, which is how the system reveals the cost of abatement.

Why are return periods flagged as not reliable?

A simulation can only estimate a return period well if it has enough years to see events of that size several times. A common rule is to require at least ten simulated years per year of return period, so 5,000 years supports return periods up to about 500 years, and 1-in-1,000 would need 10,000 years. Beyond that the estimate rests on one or two simulated years and can move a lot with the random seed, so the engine marks it rather than presenting false precision.

Why does spatial correlation change the tail but not the average?

The average loss is a sum of expectations, and expectations add up whether sites are correlated or not. The tail is different: when sites share the same storm or flood season they tend to be hit together, so bad years become worse and good years better, widening the distribution. Raising the correlation length therefore leaves AAL almost unchanged but raises the 1-in-100 loss and tail value at risk. Correlation lengths are assumptions unless fitted to event footprints, so they should be tested at low, base and high settings.

What does attribution mean when a source says an event was made more likely by climate change?

Attribution studies compare the chance of an event in today's climate with its chance in a world without human influence, using models and observations. A statement that climate change made it, for example, twice as likely is a statement about probability, not about cause in a single case. Results depend on the event definition and on how well models represent that weather type, so confidence is higher for heat than for convective rain.

What does a 1-in-100 loss mean?

A 1-in-100 loss is the loss level with a 1% chance of being exceeded in any one year. It does not mean the loss happens once every hundred years, and it does not mean it cannot happen twice in a decade. Over a 30-year horizon the chance of at least one such year is roughly one in four. Insurers often call the occurrence version the probable maximum loss, but the term has no single legal definition, so always state whether the figure is occurrence or aggregate.

What is a stranded asset?

A stranded asset is an asset that loses value before the end of its expected life because of changes tied to climate, such as a carbon price, a ban, falling demand or physical damage that makes it uneconomic. Coal plants and high-carbon industrial plants are classic transition examples; a coastal facility that can no longer be insured or defended is a physical one. The size of the loss depends on how fast the change comes and on the remaining book life.

Why is a 100-year flood a misleading name?

It describes a flood with a 1% chance of occurring in any year, not one that comes once a century. Two such floods can arrive in successive years, and over a 30-year mortgage the chance of at least one is about 26%. The estimate also changes as more data are collected and as the climate shifts, so a flood called a 100-year event today may be more frequent in future. The phrase 1% annual chance flood is clearer.

What is an SSP?

A Shared Socioeconomic Pathway describes how population, economy, energy use and policy might evolve, and each is paired with a radiative-forcing level to make a climate scenario such as SSP2-4.5. The number after the hyphen is the approximate extra forcing in watts per square metre by 2100. The IPCC's sixth assessment gives best estimates of warming for 2081 to 2100 relative to 1850 to 1900 of about 1.8 degrees for SSP1-2.6, 2.7 for SSP2-4.5, 3.6 for SSP3-7.0 and 4.4 for SSP5-8.5.

What is CBAM?

The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, Regulation (EU) 2023/956, puts a carbon price on certain imports so that they bear a cost comparable to EU producers under the Emissions Trading System. It covers cement, iron and steel, aluminium, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen. A reporting-only transitional period ran from October 2023 through 2025, and the financial obligation to surrender certificates starts with the definitive period from 2026. Thresholds and rules have been changing, so current conditions should be checked.

Why are stack emissions from a compliant cement works only a small part of the particle problem near it?

A tall stack with a filter at its legal limit releases modest amounts, and the plume mixes before it reaches the ground, so its annual contribution at a few kilometres is often a fraction of one microgram per cubic metre to a few. Much of the local burden usually comes from fugitive sources: the quarry, crushers, stockpiles, conveyors and haul roads, which are low-level and uncontrolled. A stack-only screen is therefore a lower bound for coarse particles, and the engine says so.

What does the capital proxy in the premium represent?

It estimates how much capital the site ties up: the site's average loss in the worst 1% of portfolio years minus its average loss. Capital is held for bad years, so a site that tends to lose most when the whole portfolio is having a bad year uses more capital than a site with the same average loss that fails independently. The cost of capital is applied to this amount, which is why two sites with similar AAL can carry different premiums.

Why are stack emissions from a compliant cement works only a small part of the particle problem near it?

A tall stack with a filter at its legal limit releases modest amounts, and the plume mixes before it reaches the ground, so its annual contribution at a few kilometres is often a fraction of one microgram per cubic metre to a few. Much of the local burden usually comes from fugitive sources: the quarry, crushers, stockpiles, conveyors and haul roads, which are low-level and uncontrolled. A stack-only screen is therefore a lower bound for coarse particles, and the engine says so.

How do quota share and excess-of-loss reinsurance differ?

Quota share cedes a fixed percentage of every loss, so it scales the whole distribution down and reduces average loss and tail alike in proportion. Excess-of-loss reinsurance pays only the part of a loss above an attachment point up to a limit, so it leaves small losses with the insurer and protects against big ones. Reinstatements allow a layer's limit to be restored after a payment, usually for an extra premium. Quota share is simple capital relief; excess of loss is targeted tail protection.

What is the difference between occurrence and aggregate exceedance probability?

Occurrence exceedance probability (OEP) looks at the single largest loss in each year and asks how often that largest event exceeds a given size. Aggregate exceedance probability (AEP) looks at the total of all losses in the year. AEP is always at least as large as OEP at the same probability. For a book dominated by one huge event per year they are nearly identical; when several moderate events can stack, AEP pulls ahead. Occurrence curves suit per-event reinsurance, aggregate curves suit annual capital and stop-loss covers.

Why validate a hazard model against historical events?

Validation shows whether a model reproduces what actually happened, such as observed storm tracks, recorded flood depths or tide-gauge levels, and how large the errors are. A model that cannot match the past gives little reason to trust its projections. Validation also reveals biases, such as consistent underestimation of extremes, which can then be corrected or reported. It does not prove future accuracy, but it limits the number of ways the model can be wrong.

What is an SSP?

A Shared Socioeconomic Pathway describes how population, economy, energy use and policy might evolve, and each is paired with a radiative-forcing level to make a climate scenario such as SSP2-4.5. The number after the hyphen is the approximate extra forcing in watts per square metre by 2100. The IPCC's sixth assessment gives best estimates of warming for 2081 to 2100 relative to 1850 to 1900 of about 1.8 degrees for SSP1-2.6, 2.7 for SSP2-4.5, 3.6 for SSP3-7.0 and 4.4 for SSP5-8.5.

How accurate is a digital elevation model for flood studies?

Global elevation models have vertical errors of several metres in places, and they often measure the top of buildings and vegetation rather than the ground. Flood depths are only decimetres to a couple of metres, so a few metres of error can change whether a site floods at all. Local lidar elevation data, where available, improves results a lot. Any flood depth from a global model should be treated as a screening estimate with a wide error band.

How does a deductible change the loss numbers?

A deductible removes the first slice of every loss, so it eliminates many small claims and cuts average annual loss sharply, but it hardly changes a very large event, where the deductible is a small part of the total. What is accumulation and why does it matter?

Accumulation is the build-up of exposure that can be hit by a single event, such as all insured sites inside one cyclone's wind field or one river basin. It matters because losses from nearby sites move together, so the tail of a portfolio is driven by concentration, not by the number of policies. Insurers monitor accumulation by zone, country and peril and set limits on each, because an event in the densest zone can erase many years of premium.

What is a stranded asset?

A stranded asset is an asset that loses value before the end of its expected life because of changes tied to climate, such as a carbon price, a ban, falling demand or physical damage that makes it uneconomic. Coal plants and high-carbon industrial plants are classic transition examples; a coastal facility that can no longer be insured or defended is a physical one. The size of the loss depends on how fast the change comes and on the remaining book life.

What is a marginal abatement cost curve?

A marginal abatement cost curve ranks emission-reduction measures from cheapest to most expensive per tonne of carbon dioxide avoided, with the width of each bar showing how many tonnes it removes. Measures with negative cost save money over their life. Comparing the curve with a carbon price shows which measures pay for themselves at that price and how much abatement is economic. The costs depend heavily on assumptions about energy prices, discount rates and technology.

What does a 1-in-100 loss mean?

A 1-in-100 loss is the loss level with a 1% chance of being exceeded in any one year. It does not mean the loss happens once every hundred years, and it does not mean it cannot happen twice in a decade. Over a 30-year horizon the chance of at least one such year is roughly one in four. Insurers often call the occurrence version the probable maximum loss, but the term has no single legal definition, so always state whether the figure is occurrence or aggregate.

How do quota share and excess-of-loss reinsurance differ?

Quota share cedes a fixed percentage of every loss, so it scales the whole distribution down and reduces average loss and tail alike in proportion. Excess-of-loss reinsurance pays only the part of a loss above an attachment point up to a limit, so it leaves small losses with the insurer and protects against big ones. Reinstatements allow a layer's limit to be restored after a payment, usually for an extra premium. Quota share is simple capital relief; excess of loss is targeted tail protection.

What is average annual loss?

Average annual loss (AAL) is the long-run mean of the loss in a year, found by averaging over many simulated years, including the many years with no loss at all. It is the pure-risk part of a price: what an insurer expects to pay per year before expenses, profit and a margin for uncertainty. AAL is dominated by frequent moderate events, so it says little about the tail. Two portfolios with the same AAL can have very different 1-in-100 losses, which is why AAL is always reported next to exceedance-probability figures.

What is UTCI and why does the engine build it itself?

The Universal Thermal Climate Index is the temperature of a reference calm, mild outdoor condition that would put the same thermal strain on a person as the real combination of air temperature, humidity, wind and radiation. It covers cold stress as well as heat stress. Published archives cover a limited period and cannot be queried for any coordinate, so the engine builds the index from hourly reanalysis weather for the place, from 1981 to within days of today, and counts the hours in each stress category. It is not a measured quantity, and the engine says how far it agreed with weather stations.

How does drought affect industry?

Drought cuts the water available for cooling, process use and hydropower, and can lower river levels enough to restrict barge transport. It raises the cost of water, can force reduced output, and often coincides with heat, which increases demand at the same time. What is the difference between occurrence and aggregate exceedance probability?

Occurrence exceedance probability (OEP) looks at the single largest loss in each year and asks how often that largest event exceeds a given size. Aggregate exceedance probability (AEP) looks at the total of all losses in the year. AEP is always at least as large as OEP at the same probability. For a book dominated by one huge event per year they are nearly identical; when several moderate events can stack, AEP pulls ahead. Occurrence curves suit per-event reinsurance, aggregate curves suit annual capital and stop-loss covers.

Why does sea-level rise matter more than its size suggests?

A modest rise lifts the whole baseline on which tides and surges ride, so a surge that used to be rare reaches the same height far more often. Return periods of coastal floods shrink faster than the sea-level numbers imply. Local land subsidence can add as much as the global rise, and the global figure hides large regional differences, which is why local sea-level and land-motion data are preferable when they exist.

How accurate is a digital elevation model for flood studies?

Global elevation models have vertical errors of several metres in places, and they often measure the top of buildings and vegetation rather than the ground. What is a reinstatement?

A reinstatement restores the limit of an excess-of-loss layer after it has been used, so the layer can respond again in the same period. Each reinstatement usually costs an additional premium, often a share of the original premium in proportion to the limit used. A layer with one reinstatement can pay up to twice its limit across the year. In a simulation, reinstatements matter in years with several large events, so they affect the aggregate result more than the occurrence result.
